theme: He commanded our fathers to teach their children
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 78:1-16. This psalm begins with a teacher’s voice and a plan to teach the next generation. Notice that the first verse is quoted in Matthew 13:35 as a reason Jesus spoke in parables.
settingTheScene: Psalm 78 is a long historical poem, and its first sixteen verses introduce its purpose. Asaph invites the people to listen to a “parable,” a teaching that recounts the exodus and the wilderness. Matthew applies the psalm’s opening line to Jesus: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world.” Jesus was telling the story of God’s people in a new way.
observation: “Give ear, O my people, to my teaching; incline your ears to the words of my mouth!” (v. 1).
“I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings from of old” (v. 2).
“We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD” (v. 4).
“He established a testimony in Jacob and appointed a law in Israel” (v. 5).
“That the next generation might know them, the children yet unborn” (v. 6).
“So that they should set their hope in God and not forget the works of God” (v. 7).
“The Ephraimites, armed with bows, turned back on the day of battle” (v. 9).
“He divided the sea and let them pass through it, and made the waters stand like a heap” (v. 13).
interpretation:
The psalm is a lesson in how faith is passed on. The speaker says that what we have heard and known, and what our fathers told us, we will not hide from our children. God commanded the fathers to teach their children, so that each generation would know and set hope in God, and not be like their stubborn ancestors. The goal is not information alone, but hope, remembrance, and obedience.

Then the psalm gives a negative example: the Ephraimites, who were armed and yet turned back in battle because they “did not keep God’s covenant.” They forgot his works. The rest of the psalm, which you will read later, is a catalog of Israel’s forgetfulness.

The first verses of the history begin with the exodus. God divided the sea, led them with a cloud by day and fire by night, and split rocks in the wilderness to give them water “abundantly as the deep.” These are wonders that should have inspired lasting trust.

Matthew quotes the psalm’s opening in 13:35 to explain Jesus’ parables. The parable of the Sower came right before. Jesus was now doing what Asaph said: opening his mouth in parables and uttering what had been hidden. And the content was the story of Israel retold. The King was both the teacher and the fulfillment of the story.

For parents, teachers, and the children’s ministry, this psalm is a charter. The purpose of teaching is that the next generation will “set their hope in God.” Tell the stories. Do not hide them.
connection: Matthew 13:34-35 quotes verse 2 as fulfilled in Jesus. Deuteronomy 6:6-7 commands teaching the words of God to your children. Exodus 14 and 17 are the events recalled. Proverbs 22:6 says to train up a child in the way he should go. 2 Timothy 1:5 and 3:14-15 describe faith passed through grandmother and mother. Ephesians 6:4 tells fathers to bring up their children in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. Joel 1:3: tell your children of it.
application:
Tell one younger person, a child, a grandchild, a student, or a new believer, a story of what God has done.

Write down three works of God in your own life, so you will not forget them.

If you serve with children, pray for the next generation to set their hope in God.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to help you pass on what you have heard and known.
Confess where you hide his deeds from the next generation.
Thank him for those who taught you.
